description_full: Ibotta, Inc., a technology company, provides digital promotion services to clients in the United States. The company sources digital promotions from its clients primarily consumer packaged goods brands and distributes these promotions to consumers through its network of publishers enabled by Ibotta Performance Network (IPN), a technology platform. It offers promotional services through the IPN, including direct-to-consumer mobile, web, and browser extension properties, as well as third-party publisher properties. The company also provides display ads, tiles, sponsored offers, newsletters, and feature placements. In addition, it offers LiveLift, a set of capabilities designed for brands to drive sales. The company serves consumer packaged goods brands. The company was formerly known as Zing Enterprises, Inc. and changed its name to Ibotta, Inc. in 2012. Ibotta, Inc. was incorporated in 2011 and is headquartered in Denver, Colorado.

financial_summary: Ibotta, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $1.3B market cap on $342M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -7.8pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 83% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $75M in free cash flow — roughly 22 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 26.65× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin -1.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 18.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and stock-based comp at 13% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insiders hold 43% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
